Dam Pipe

By: Anna-Maria van Niekerk | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Despite a year's fight and the crippling drought, the pipe that will take partially treated sewage effluent into the Vaal Dam is set to go ahead, as the Dam level drops by 10cm a day...

Unique Selling Point:
After a year of fighting to prevent the construction of a pipeline from Deneysville’s sewage works into the Vaal Dam, residents have just discovered the shocking news that their objections have been steamrollered and the pipe will go ahead – precisely where it had been laid in secret, and poorly constructed to boot. Now the pipe will stay where it's been laid because there's ostensibly no money to move it...but where it enters what used to be the Vaal Dam, is now dry land, thanks to the drought.

The Vaal Dam holds the drinking water for the country’s most densely populated economic heartland is only 33% full and the water level drops by 10cm a day. Not only is the precious resource threatened by the drought but what little water is left is threatened by what residents feel will be wilful pollution by the local municipality.

But not only is it Deneysville's pipe and partially treated effluent that's affecting the Vaal Dam, sewage treatment works all along the catchment, up to Villiers, that have been the subject of Carte Blanche scrutiny, have come in for pressure to fix faltering treatment works. But while construction work in Standerton and Frankfort give reason for hope, Villiers is in a worse state than ever, and new reports are emerging.

In August 2015 Minister of Water and Sanitation Nomvula Mokonyane announced the construction of the Sedibeng Regional Sewer System – a mega sewage plant to take care of sewage spills at the three existing, old and overworked sewage plants in the South of Johannesburg. It would have been up and running within three years. Identified by the Presidential Infrastructure Coordinating Council as early as 2005, it now appears that the mega waterworks has now been postponed.

The United Nations Environment Programme last week issued a report on the Vaal River basin -- flagging it for salinity from acid mine drainage, eutrophication and pollution from microbiological causes -- like defunct sewage works.

The Department of Water and Sanitation's way of dealing with pollution has always been to dilute it out, by releasing water from the dam to flush the Barrage and Vaal as it proceeds into the Free State and flows into the Orange River, but with the persisting drought and the unrelenting pollution of sewage works, as well as acid mine drainage from mines along the Upper Vaal, and the release of partially treated AMD back into the Vaal and Crocodile rivers, what has long been predicted is now reality -- the Vaal Dam is losing its dilution capacity and it's only a matter of time before consumers bear the brunt of increased treatment costs.

DWS DG Margaret-Ann Diedricks promised Carte Blanche a road-trip to show off their progress in fixing problems in the Upper Vaal by April this year, but all that happened, despite numerous attempts to arrange this interview, is that the Director-General was ousted from her post, the Minister of Water is being investigated by the Public Protector on various corruption allegations, and in Deneysville the ANC municipality lost its hold on the council in the municipal elections -- the town is now under a DA-led coalition.

In this story we aim to recap what's happened to the pipe -- asking the new municipal leaders to open the books and tell us where things went so wrong; holding accountable the environmental practitioners that promised to keep the community informed; and the contractor who is accused of shoddy workmanship on the pipe.

We will try to present the best forecasts of what weather patterns say about coming rain and what the drought and pollution levels mean for the Vaal in coming months.

The Vaal's fate is at a critical point and we will analyse the big picture of how problems like Deneysville contribute to the degradation of the Vaal system.

Summary:
Deneysville’s activists discovered (at the end of August) that approval for the pipe’s Water Use Licence was given in April already without any feedback or notification after they were engaged in a public consultation process. Worst of all, the Water Use Licence seems to have been given for 5 years, while the sewage treatment works still have to be upgraded to handle the massive population increase in the area. For now, the effluent that is discharged in the Vaal is not compliant with legislated treatment levels.

After the activists had worked to get the issue aired in the media, the local council came under severe pressure by the national Department of Water and Sanitation to fill highly dangerous open trenches and flooded pump stations. The hazardous trenches were filled and partially treated sewage is now diverted into a massive unfenced quarry -- in which a child drowned last year. But despite their initial doubts, the residents have come to accept the quarry and it would seem that the quarry holds water that is attracting bird life and might be suitable for cultivating grass and creating employment.

They would prefer this to what they’ve now been told will happen: The pipe will be re-opened where it had hastily been installed and merely covered to allow for a consultation process that residents feel was a total waste of time.

Residents accuse DWS and the local council of acting in bad faith by never giving the interested and affected parties who had attended the community meeting any feedback, and trying to hide the (hot potato) issue in the run-up to local elections and to prevent the residents from appealing the outcome – they would have had a limited time to appeal after the decision was made final.

But what DWS and the municipality probably haven't bargained on is a Cape Supreme Court ruling that the 30-day appeal period can only start once the affected parties become aware of the decision; not from the day of the official decision.

Press Release:


Vaal Dam: Status Critical
The Vaal Dam is rapidly drying up and with the drought worsening each day, severe water restrictions are on the cards. The public have been warned that they will be fined for wastage or excessive water use, but what about the municipalities routinely mismanaging and polluting existing water resources? Are authorities equally committed to cleaning up their act? Carte Blanche heads back to the Vaal to see if promised infrastructure improvements are being implemented.


Script:


DAM PIPE
At the harbor in Deneysville on the Vaal Dam, Kathy Manten hasn’t seen a drought this bad since 1995.
KATHY MANTEN, DENEYSVILLE RESIDENT: Sad loss of water. Big drought. No-one could really predict it. At least half of our members’ boats are standing on the hard on cradles. We’ve lost a couple of inches in one day earlier on this week just from hot wind and sun. You drop every day; you can see that much.
DEREK LINK: The Vaal Dam is just about a third full but the bigger problem is that the pollutants haven’t decreased and there’s not enough water to wash them away.
It’s a situation we warned about last year when we investigated the sorry state of sewage works along the Vaal Dam and the rivers that feed it. We discovered pump stations blocked and flooded… people forced to live in the pungent mess.
UPS 2015; SHAN HOLMES: …This is a time-bomb with a not so long fuse…where we are going to deliberately and knowingly shoot up the costs of water and impact on our water availability.
DEREK LINK: A year ago the DG of water and sanitation, Margaret Ann Diedricks, promised to take us on the road to look at progress with sewage management systems along the Vaal River and Dam. This never happened as she left the department after a very short tenure.
UPSOUND: 2015 STORY: MARGARET-ANN DIEDRICKS: I can certainly commit to joining you on that roadshow to show the progress and I think the minister will have no problem in joining us as well.
DEREK: Margaret-Ann Diedricks gave us great hope for the future…why did she leave?
SPUTNIK RATAU, SPOKESMAN: DEPARTMENT OF WATER AND SANITATION: That is a discussion for the Minister and the former DG. I cannot respond to that. DGs and Ministers deal with themselves at that level.
Now, water restrictions grip the country. We will be fined for using too much, says Minister of Water and Sanitation Nomvula Mokonyane. But who will hold government to account for wasting precious drops?
MINISTER BRIEFING: We are one of the driest countries in the world – we do have a possibility of living with the little that we have if we manage the little that we have…
Vaal Marina resident turned water warrior Irene Main gives credit where it’s due.
DEREK: Irene, our last program about a year ago…what’s happened since then?
IRENE MAIN, MEMBER: SAVE THE VAAL ENVIRONMENT: Water Affairs has started an emergency intervention program where they have allocated R330 million to basically fix what is not working at 26 wastewater treatment plants – most of them are in the Vaal catchment area. That’s proceeding nicely. If you have a look at Deneysville now compared to a year ago, there’s not sewage lying around and it’s not in the homes of the people in Refengkgotso. It’s a hell of a lot better.
But despite some outward improvements, test points monitored throughout the Vaal catchment prove that levels of E.coli, salts and other contaminants in the water coming from sewage plants are still unacceptably high. Rand Water’s charts bleed red where pollutants exceed what’s acceptable.
And new leaks keep popping up – Gary Colegate joined SAVE to help fight the demise of Emfuleni’s pipelines in Vereeniging and Vanderbijlpark pump.
UPS at PUMP STATION
GARY COLEGATE, MEMBER: SAVE THE VAAL ENVIRONMENT: Unfortunately you can see this hasn’t been attended to for some time. Despite the efforts of organisations like ourselves – SAVE – most cases I’m afraid complaints fall on deaf ears.
DEREK LINK: This is what you’d call politely an extreme health hazard – raw sewage floating alongside a public road, cattle eating it and drinking the water before it flows down a few hundred meters to the Vaal River.
The United Nations Environment Program just listed the Vaal – and Limpopo Rivers – as pollution hotspots, just as water scientist Shan Holmes always said would happen.
DR SHAN HOLMES, ENVIRONMENTAL SCIENTIST: The report is entirely correct in pointing out that these major rivers that we’re very dependent on are in fact highly polluted. As soon as you get a drought situation with levels dropping that pollution problem that sits there all the time, is heavily exacerbated.
SAMSON MOKOENA, FOUNDER: VAAL ENVIRONMENTAL JUSTICE ALLIANCE: When you get kids that play in this polluted sewer water, then think about skin rash and other diseases, think about millions of South Africans who uses that resources for spiritual and healing purposes.
Emfuleni resident Samson Mokoena says they’ve needed high-level intervention and new sewage plants years ago already, but he feels people are just not heard.
SAMSON MOKOENA, FOUNDER: VAAL ENVIRONMENTAL JUSTICE ALLIANCE: We’re sitting in this long meetings for year after year, year after year. But we see lack of action in terms of cleaning the water. What we’ve noticed for the last 15, 20 years is that we’ve had lots of good laws, but we’ve seen government failing to implement those laws.
For Gary Colegate the root of the evil is money, especially in the Emfuleni Municipality.
GARY COLEGATE, MEMBER: SAVE THE VAAL ENVIRONMENT: And then you’ve got a deficit, in excess of R500 million it is, I think it’s R571 million, compared to the previous financial year when it was R178 million. So yes, we are concerned.
Amid dire financial straits, Emfuleni municipality’s acting chief director for utilities Ernie Strydom has to keep the aging system going.
ERNIE STRYDOM, ACTING CHIEF DIRECTOR: UTILITIES, EMFULENI LOCAL MUNICIPALITY: We sit with old infrastructure, some of the infrastructure is older than 70 years.
While Emfuleni is repairing what it can with what it’s got, hopes were really pinned on a new multi-billion rand MEGA WORKS, dubbed the Sedibeng Regional Sewerage Scheme, in the south of Gauteng.
SAMSON MOKOENA, FOUNDER: VAAL ENVIRONMENTAL JUSTICE ALLIANCE: We were excited because it was going to solve some of the big problems that we have in terms of capacity of local government in terms of treating the water.
ERNIE STRYDOM, ACTING CHIEF DIRECTOR: UTILITIES, EMFULENI LOCAL MUNICIPALITY: The regional scheme was already on the cards since 2005. It’s supposed to move faster.
But now, the money is needed elsewhere. This week National Treasury told us the national grant which would partially fund the mega-works has been cut by almost half a billion rand to go toward other priorities like higher education.
ERNIE STRYDOM, ACTING CHIEF DIRECTOR: UTILITIES, EMFULENI LOCAL MUNICIPALITY: If the funding was withdrawn, I don’t think Emfuleni is aware of that currently.
Back in Deneysville, residents were shocked to learn last month that a pipeline they fought against tooth and nail and managed to get halted temporarily, got the green light from national government to operate for five years. It will take treated effluent from the plant into the Vaal, to the dismay of retiree and pollution watchdog Peet Schabort.
PEET SCHABORT: People using the water of the Vaal Dam at this moment – they’re sitting in Vanderbijlpark or in Johannesburg; they don’t know how serious it is here.
Aquatic scientist Stephen van Staden was in charge of the community consultation and environmental impact assessment to say whether the pipe should be put into use.
STEPHEN VAN STADEN, MANAGING DIRECTOR: SCIENTIFIC AQUATIC SERVICES: There was a number of alternatives investigated. This was determined to be the best alternative considering all the options.
In the long run the plant that now copes with less than half the sewage it receives, must be expanded to treat water to acceptable standard. In the meantime, the dam is the where it will go – there’s no money to move the pipe.
STEPHEN VAN STADEN: We need to get rid of this partially treated effluent while the works is being upgraded – so there will be a period when effluent that is not being treated to the required standard will be discharged.
DEREK: Into the dam?
STEPHEN VAN STADEN: Into the dam…
KATHY MANTEN, DENEYSVILLE RESIDENT: It comes out into the dam in an area where there’s not big water flow. There’s not a lot of movement in the water. All of that water with the impurities and the unpurified sewage is going to back up in that bay.
DR SHAN HOLMES, ENVIRONMENTAL SCIENTIST: This is a medieval practice of running effluent into really what is one’s strategic and critical drinking water.
DEREK: We’re told, oh, there’s no problem with decanting it into the Vaal if it’s of a certain quality of effluent.
DR SHAN HOLMES, ENVIRONMENTAL SCIENTIST: So you’re giving a critical effluent quality and water quality function over to a small municipality and a bio-monitoring function over to a small municipality – and the question is, do our small municipalities have the skills to do this water monitoring and are they going to implement and take the management decisions that are required?
The last hope for the activists is the new DA-led coalition, elected into power in the local municipality last month – just because the pipe’s been approved, doesn’t mean they have to use it, says Mayor Sello Hlasa.
SELLO HLASA, METSIMAHOLO MAYOR: We need to review, we need to sit down with all our specialities who are working on this thing and we need to go and do a site visit so that they explain to us – I’m not an engineer…but I can tell when there’s bad engineering. Immediately when you hear there is a problem next to the Vaal Dam that has to do with sewage, really, you must be worried.
Water and Sanitation Department spokesman Sputnik Ratau.
DEREK: Government prides itself on taking water to the people but it’s not much use if it’s polluted and undrinkable.
SPUTNIK RATAU, SPOKESMAN: DEPARTMENT OF WATER AND SANITATION: Capacity, especially within smaller municipalities – even if there was infrastructure initially but after a while the quality starts being impacted upon and it’s not something that government is very proud of because the idea is that by the time we get to universal access, it has to be universal access of good quality water.
The South African Weather Service says below-normal rainfall and above-normal temperatures will continue throughout spring. A weak La Niña weather pattern is possible in early summer. La Niña usually brings heavy rains but this one may yet fizzle out.
KATHY MANTEN, DENEYSVILLE RESIDENT: That’s been Water Affairs’ saving grace is the fact that they’ve had a lot of water to try and dilute and wash the world clean. They don’t have a lot of water to wash the world clean anymore. They need to start looking after the little bit they’ve got.

GARY COLEGATE, MEMBER: SAVE THE VAAL ENVIRONMENT: And then you’ve got a deficit, in excess of R500 million it is, I think it’s R571 million, compared to the previous financial year when it was R178 million. So yes, we are concerned. Amid dire financial straits, Emfuleni municipality’s acting chief director for utilities Ernie Strydom has to keep the aging system going. ERNIE STRYDOM, ACTING CHIEF DIRECTOR: UTILITIES, EMFULENI LOCAL MUNICIPALITY: We sit with old infrastructure, some of the infrastructure is older than 70 years. While Emfuleni is repairing what it can with what it’s got, hopes were really pinned on a new multi-billion rand MEGA WORKS, dubbed the Sedibeng Regional Sewerage Scheme, in the south of Gauteng. SAMSON MOKOENA, FOUNDER: VAAL ENVIRONMENTAL JUSTICE ALLIANCE: We were excited because it was going to solve some of the big problems that we have in terms of capacity of local government in terms of treating the water. ERNIE STRYDOM, ACTING CHIEF DIRECTOR: UTILITIES, EMFULENI LOCAL MUNICIPALITY: The regional scheme was already on the cards since 2005. It’s supposed to move faster. But now, the money is needed elsewhere. This week National Treasury told us the national grant which would partially fund the mega-works has been cut by almost half a billion rand to go toward other priorities like higher education. ERNIE STRYDOM, ACTING CHIEF DIRECTOR: UTILITIES, EMFULENI LOCAL MUNICIPALITY: If the funding was withdrawn, I don’t think Emfuleni is aware of that currently. Back in Deneysville, residents were shocked to learn last month that a pipeline they fought against tooth and nail and managed to get halted temporarily, got the green light from national government to operate for five years. It will take treated effluent from the plant into the Vaal, to the dismay of retiree and pollution watchdog Peet Schabort. PEET SCHABORT: People using the water of the Vaal Dam at this moment – they’re sitting in Vanderbijlpark or in Johannesburg; they don’t know how serious it is here. Aquatic scientist Stephen van Staden was in charge of the community consultation and environmental impact assessment to say whether the pipe should be put into use. STEPHEN VAN STADEN, MANAGING DIRECTOR: SCIENTIFIC AQUATIC SERVICES: There was a number of alternatives investigated. This was determined to be the best alternative considering all the options. In the long run the plant that now copes with less than half the sewage it receives, must be expanded to treat water to acceptable standard. In the meantime, the dam is the where it will go – there’s no money to move the pipe. STEPHEN VAN STADEN: We need to get rid of this partially treated effluent while the works is being upgraded – so there will be a period when effluent that is not being treated to the required standard will be discharged. DEREK: Into the dam? STEPHEN VAN STADEN: Into the dam… KATHY MANTEN, DENEYSVILLE RESIDENT: It comes out into the dam in an area where there’s not big water flow. There’s not a lot of movement in the water. All of that water with the impurities and the unpurified sewage is going to back up in that bay. DR SHAN HOLMES, ENVIRONMENTAL SCIENTIST: This is a medieval practice of running effluent into really what is one’s strategic and critical drinking water. DEREK: We’re told, oh, there’s no problem with decanting it into the Vaal if it’s of a certain quality of effluent. DR SHAN HOLMES, ENVIRONMENTAL SCIENTIST: So you’re giving a critical effluent quality and water quality function over to a small municipality and a bio-monitoring function over to a small municipality – and the question is, do our small municipalities have the skills to do this water monitoring and are they going to implement and take the management decisions that are required? The last hope for the activists is the new DA-led coalition, elected into power in the local municipality last month – just because the pipe’s been approved, doesn’t mean they have to use it, says Mayor Sello Hlasa. SELLO HLASA, METSIMAHOLO MAYOR: We need to review, we need to sit down with all our specialities who are working on this thing and we need to go and do a site visit so that they explain to us – I’m not an engineer…but I can tell when there’s bad engineering. Immediately when you hear there is a problem next to the Vaal Dam that has to do with sewage, really, you must be worried. Water and Sanitation Department spokesman Sputnik Ratau. DEREK: Government prides itself on taking water to the people but it’s not much use if it’s polluted and undrinkable. SPUTNIK RATAU, SPOKESMAN: DEPARTMENT OF WATER AND SANITATION: Capacity, especially within smaller municipalities – even if there was infrastructure initially but after a while the quality starts being impacted upon and it’s not something that government is very proud of because the idea is that by the time we get to universal access, it has to be universal access of good quality water. The South African Weather Service says below-normal rainfall and above-normal temperatures will continue throughout spring. A weak La Niña weather pattern is possible in early summer. La Niña usually brings heavy rains but this one may yet fizzle out. KATHY MANTEN, DENEYSVILLE RESIDENT: That’s been Water Affairs’ saving grace is the fact that they’ve had a lot of water to try and dilute and wash the world clean. They don’t have a lot of water to wash the world clean anymore. They need to start looking after the little bit they’ve got.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Despite a year's fight and the crippling drought, the pipe that will take partially treated sewage effluent into the Vaal Dam is set to go ahead, as the Dam level drops by 10cm a day...
metadata.Unique Selling Point: After a year of fighting to prevent the construction of a pipeline from Deneysville’s sewage works into the Vaal Dam, residents have just discovered the shocking news that their objections have been steamrollered and the pipe will go ahead – precisely where it had been laid in secret, and poorly constructed to boot. Now the pipe will stay where it's been laid because there's ostensibly no money to move it...but where it enters what used to be the Vaal Dam, is now dry land, thanks to the drought. The Vaal Dam holds the drinking water for the country’s most densely populated economic heartland is only 33% full and the water level drops by 10cm a day. Not only is the precious resource threatened by the drought but what little water is left is threatened by what residents feel will be wilful pollution by the local municipality. But not only is it Deneysville's pipe and partially treated effluent that's affecting the Vaal Dam, sewage treatment works all along the catchment, up to Villiers, that have been the subject of Carte Blanche scrutiny, have come in for pressure to fix faltering treatment works. But while construction work in Standerton and Frankfort give reason for hope, Villiers is in a worse state than ever, and new reports are emerging. In August 2015 Minister of Water and Sanitation Nomvula Mokonyane announced the construction of the Sedibeng Regional Sewer System – a mega sewage plant to take care of sewage spills at the three existing, old and overworked sewage plants in the South of Johannesburg. It would have been up and running within three years. Identified by the Presidential Infrastructure Coordinating Council as early as 2005, it now appears that the mega waterworks has now been postponed. The United Nations Environment Programme last week issued a report on the Vaal River basin -- flagging it for salinity from acid mine drainage, eutrophication and pollution from microbiological causes -- like defunct sewage works. The Department of Water and Sanitation's way of dealing with pollution has always been to dilute it out, by releasing water from the dam to flush the Barrage and Vaal as it proceeds into the Free State and flows into the Orange River, but with the persisting drought and the unrelenting pollution of sewage works, as well as acid mine drainage from mines along the Upper Vaal, and the release of partially treated AMD back into the Vaal and Crocodile rivers, what has long been predicted is now reality -- the Vaal Dam is losing its dilution capacity and it's only a matter of time before consumers bear the brunt of increased treatment costs. DWS DG Margaret-Ann Diedricks promised Carte Blanche a road-trip to show off their progress in fixing problems in the Upper Vaal by April this year, but all that happened, despite numerous attempts to arrange this interview, is that the Director-General was ousted from her post, the Minister of Water is being investigated by the Public Protector on various corruption allegations, and in Deneysville the ANC municipality lost its hold on the council in the municipal elections -- the town is now under a DA-led coalition. In this story we aim to recap what's happened to the pipe -- asking the new municipal leaders to open the books and tell us where things went so wrong; holding accountable the environmental practitioners that promised to keep the community informed; and the contractor who is accused of shoddy workmanship on the pipe. We will try to present the best forecasts of what weather patterns say about coming rain and what the drought and pollution levels mean for the Vaal in coming months. The Vaal's fate is at a critical point and we will analyse the big picture of how problems like Deneysville contribute to the degradation of the Vaal system.
metadata.Summary: Deneysville’s activists discovered (at the end of August) that approval for the pipe’s Water Use Licence was given in April already without any feedback or notification after they were engaged in a public consultation process. Worst of all, the Water Use Licence seems to have been given for 5 years, while the sewage treatment works still have to be upgraded to handle the massive population increase in the area. For now, the effluent that is discharged in the Vaal is not compliant with legislated treatment levels. After the activists had worked to get the issue aired in the media, the local council came under severe pressure by the national Department of Water and Sanitation to fill highly dangerous open trenches and flooded pump stations. The hazardous trenches were filled and partially treated sewage is now diverted into a massive unfenced quarry -- in which a child drowned last year. But despite their initial doubts, the residents have come to accept the quarry and it would seem that the quarry holds water that is attracting bird life and might be suitable for cultivating grass and creating employment. They would prefer this to what they’ve now been told will happen: The pipe will be re-opened where it had hastily been installed and merely covered to allow for a consultation process that residents feel was a total waste of time. Residents accuse DWS and the local council of acting in bad faith by never giving the interested and affected parties who had attended the community meeting any feedback, and trying to hide the (hot potato) issue in the run-up to local elections and to prevent the residents from appealing the outcome – they would have had a limited time to appeal after the decision was made final. But what DWS and the municipality probably haven't bargained on is a Cape Supreme Court ruling that the 30-day appeal period can only start once the affected parties become aware of the decision; not from the day of the official decision.
